sweep_summary: this search of works with stress in the title's single item, Pittman 1970 'Gurung, Tamang, Thakali, Sherpa, and Chepang prosodies' (Hale & Pike Part II, pp. 1-8), was downloaded from the ERIC ED046002 microfiche scan on archive.org and read in full: it concerns the four register/pitch classes of monosyllabic word-bases and their consonant-voicing origin, mentions stress only for Tamang, and is silent on Gurung word-stress placement (priority none). As a by-product the Part I volume (ERIC ED046001, archive.org item micro_IA41153125_0126, mislabelled in IA metadata) yielded the published Glover 1970 'Gurung tone and higher levels' (pp. 52-73) whose 'Stress' section (p. 72) repeats verbatim the catalog's deciding passage (non-phonemic slight primary stress on the first syllable of the foot/word; secondary stress on the pitch-accented syllable), and Pike 1970 (p. 40) independently confirms initial demarcative stress with the contrastive-stress hypothesis rejected. catalog's classification fixed-strict initial is confirmed; no contradicting statement found. Glover & Glover 1972 'A guide to Gurung tone' remains unread (SIL: not online; HathiTrust search-only), low priority. discovery ran through archive.org, ERIC API, SIL archive pages (via the Internet Archive listing) and the HathiTrust volumes API (babel.hathitrust.org could not be reached by automated download). Everything downloaded is under and logged in there.

new_statements.quote: Word stress is not phonemic in Gurung--that is, it does not establish contrastive units (except for the presence of secondary stress on the accented syllable if in first or second position in the word, as described above). However the first syllable of a foot regularly carries a slight stress (primary by comparison with the secondary stress on the accented syllable), which serves as a characteristic feature distinguishing the foot, as a level, from the next lower, the syllable, and the next higher, the phonological phrase.

Pike (eds.), Tone systems of Tibeto-Burman languages of Nepal, Part I: Studies on tone and phonological segments (Occasional Papers of the Wolfenden Society on Tibeto-Burman Linguistics 3:1), 52-73. new_statements.reading: Fixed, non-contrastive, weak primary stress on the first syllable of the foot (= phonological word); the lexical high-pitch 'accent' can sit on any syllable and is a pitch contrast, not stress (it carries only a secondary stress when in 1st/2nd position). This is the published form of the very passage the catalog quotes from the 1969 SIL mimeo, so the catalog's fixed-strict initial coding stands; Pike 1970 (p. 40) independently reports the same initial demarcative stress and notes that a contrastive-stress hypothesis was tested and rejected.

tone_statements.citation: Ronkos, Danielle. 2015. Obstruent Voicing and Tone in Siklis Gurung. MA thesis, The Graduate Center, City University of New York (CUNY Academic Works gc_etds/1110).
tone_statements.quote: There seem to be three identifiable tones: a very low tone that occurs with breathy vowels, a mid-tone with optionally slightly-breathy vowels, and a high tone with clear vowels. I will number them from 1 to 3 with 1 representing the highest tone and 3 representing the lowest tone. … this suggests that there are three distinct pitch levels in Siklis Gurung that can be characterized as three separate tone categories. … This makes for a three-tone system: tone 1 is high with a clear vowel, tone 2 is mid with a clear vowel, and tone 3 is markedly low with a breathy vowel.
tone_statements.locator: Sec. 4.4 'Tones of Siklis Gurung', pp.34-35 + 7.0 Conclusion p.40
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones on the phonological word: high and mid with clear vowels, low with breathy voice; whether the tones have contours is left open; one speaker of Siklis (Kaski) Gurung.

tone_statements.quote: Three Gurung Tone Models: … Kaski Gurung … (Glover 1974) … Tone 1 “clear, relaxed” … Tone 2 “clear, intense” … Tone 3 “breathy, low” … Tone 4 “breathy, rising” … authoritative, long-standing … reference for Gurung tone … • Pitch-melody: Four Manang-Gurung speakers (5 measurement points) … • M-G: a high-low separation only emerges when plotted against Manange model for 3 of 4 speakers so far … • While still quite tentative … this talk represents a !rst view to a systematic comparative examination of the phonetic manifestation of tone in these languages

tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Tests F0 and voice quality of four Manang Gurung speakers against earlier four-tone models (Glover: clear relaxed, clear intense, breathy low, breathy rising); only a tentative high-low split emerges.

tone_statements.citation: Hildebrandt, Kristine A. 2009. Gurung (Tibeto-Burman) at the tonogenetic crossroads. Paper presented at the 15th Mid-Continental Workshop on Phonology, Indiana University, Bloomington, 10 October 2009 (handout on academia.edu 2401616).
tone_statements.quote: Kaski Gurung … (Glover 1974) … Tone 1 “clear, relaxed” … Tone 2 “clear, intense” … Tone 3 “breathy, low” … Tone 4 “breathy, rising” … The acoustic picture at this point is scattered and non-uniform: … A loose (but unreliable x-speakers) F0 alignment between M-G … and Kaski or Manange … M-G speakers appear to be very good (better … than average) at distinguishing segmental homophones with no … contextual cues … If Manang-Gurung lacks any type of suprasegmental system akin to … Tamangic tone, this is a recent and dramatic case of de-linking
tone_statements.locator: Slide 11 'Tone Models' table, slide 34 'Discussion', slide 38 'Final Remarks'
tone_statements.summary: Cites Glover's (1974) four Kaski Gurung tones: 1 clear relaxed, 2 clear intense, 3 breathy low, 4 breathy rising; acoustic test on Manang Gurung finds only loose F0 alignment; tonal status left open.

tone_statements.citation: Mazaudon, Martine. 2005. On tone in Tamang and neighbouring languages: synchrony and diachrony. In Shigeki Kaji (ed.), Proceedings of the Symposium Cross-linguistic Studies of Tonal Phenomena: Historical development, tone-syntax interface, and descriptive studies, 79-96. Tokyo: ILCAA, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies.
tone_statements.quote: In TGTM languages the tone bearing unit in the lexicon is the morpheme; in the sentence, it is the word, formed of a tonal lexical item plus its atonal grammatical affixes. … All languages of the Tamang branch described until now2 exhibit a four-tone system (Mazaudon M., 1978). … Five of the eight dialects listed have a main split in their system between two high tones and two low tones. These are Risiangku and Sahugaon Tamang, Tukche and Syang Thakali, and Ghachok Gurung. Correlatively, the low tones are accompanied by a particular phonation type, which has been described as breathiness
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2.2 and 2.2.1 with Fig. 1 'Phonetic pitch of the 4 tones on monosyllables in 8 dialects of the TGTM group' (GURUNG Ghachok column: 1. 33, 2. 54, 3. 11, 4. 12), manuscript pp. 3-4
tone_statements.summary: Four word-tones (Ghachok pitch 33, 54, 11, 12); tones 3-4 low and breathy; the word (root plus toneless suffixes) carries one melody; TGTM syllables said to be equally prominent, no accent.

tone_statements.citation: Sprigg, R. K. 1997. A tonal analysis of Gurung, with separate systems for register and contour pitch features. Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 60(3): 448-454.
tone_statements.quote: to the speech of Manshiri Gurungni, of Thak (or Thonsu), towards the centre of the Gurung-speaking area, I found that I could apply the same tonal analysis as for Tamang at (III) above: two tone systems, each comprising … two terms, register tones 1 and 2 and contour tones A and B … this suffix lexical item occurs in words of all four tone combinations, 1-and-A, 1-and-B, 2-and-A, and 2-and-B … word tone: 1-and-A 1-and-B 2-and-A 2-and-B pitches: high high low low level falling falling/level rising-falling/level examples: shi- khru- pri- byo-
tone_statements.locator: Sec. IV.A 'Register difference and contour difference', pp. 450-451 (page header at l.213 skipped), 246-248, 260-263
tone_statements.summary: Word-based tone analysed as two two-term systems, register (1 = high, 2 = low) and contour (A, B): four word tones, high level, high falling, low falling/level, low rising-falling/level.

tone_statements.citation: Mazaudon, Martine. 1978. Consonantal mutation and tonal split in the Tamang sub-family of Tibeto-Burman. Kailash: A Journal of Himalayan Studies 6(3): 157-179.
tone_statements.quote: Each monosyllabic word, in languages of the TGTM group, can carry one of four tones. … the languages of the TGTM group do not distinguish four tones on each syllable of a word … but only four tones per word. … In five dialects out of eight, Risiangku and Sahu Tamang, Tukche and Syang Thakali, and Ghachok Gurung, tone-1 and tone-2 words ‘are high with a clear voice quality; tone-3 and tone-4 are low with a breathy voice quality. The opposition of tone-1 to tone-2, and that of tone-3 to tone-4 rest on a combination of melody and relative pitch which varies with each dialect.
tone_statements.locator: sec.2.1 p.160, sec.2.4 p.163, sec.3.1 p.164; Ghachok values in table sec.3.12 p.165
tone_statements.summary: Four tones per word, not per syllable: tone-1, tone-2 high with clear voice, tone-3, tone-4 low and breathy (Ghachok 33, 54, 11, 12); suffixes toneless; five patterns seen on disyllabic nouns.

tone_statements.citation: Glover, Warren W. 1971. Register in Tibeto-Burman languages of Nepal: a comparison with Mon-Khmer. In Papers in South East Asian Linguistics No. 2 (Pacific Linguistics A-29), 1-22. Canberra: Australian National University.
tone_statements.quote: The classification according to these variables of monosyllabic nouns, verb roots, and numerals produced four sets which fell clearly into two groups of two sets each: a clear group, comprising intense and relaxed sets, and a breathy group, comprising rising and low sets. … in minimal contrasts between the sets there is a consistent pattern of pitch in terms of three levels. The four sets, with typical identifying features and examples, are listed in Table 1. … The breathy group in both Gurung and Thakali is further subdivided by contrastive contour versus low level pitch
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2.1, p. 6; Table 1 'Contrastive sets in Gurung' p. 7 (: Pitch High / Mid / Low-mid glide / Low); last clause sec. 2.2 point (3), p. 14
tone_statements.summary: Monosyllables contrast four sets: clear intense (high), clear relaxed (mid), breathy rising, breathy low, i.e. clear/breathy register crossed with pitch; longer words are described by a pitch accent.

tone_statements.quote: TT was a "four-box" register language, which means that each word-base (WB) is interpreted as having had two syllables, each of which had back (tense) or front (lax) tongue-root articulation. … Stress, relative pitch, pitch contour, intensity and breathiness carry a high proportion of the functional load of the register system in T, Gu, and Th. the prosodic features of the three languages are realized as follows; … Gu word-bases may be om clear intense, (b) clear relaxed, (3) breathy rising, or (da) breathy low pitch.
tone_statements.locator: Pittman & Glover sec. 1, pp. 9-10; same four classes in Pittman 'prosodies' sec. 1 Table 1, p. 1.
tone_statements.summary: Four word-base prosodies (clear intense, clear relaxed, breathy rising, breathy low), analysed as tense/lax register combinations KK, KG, GK, GG; realised by pitch, voice quality, stress, intensity.

tone_statements.citation: Burton-Page, J. 1955. Two studies in Gurungkura: I. Tone; II. Rhotacization and retroflexion. Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 17(1): 111-119.
tone_statements.quote: Words in the main system—i.e. those which are not to be recognized as loanwords from Nepali—may be stated in terms of a two-term tone system as … ‘tone 1’ and ‘tone 2’ words. Loanwords from Nepali, which Ganesh used freely, aro more conveniently assigned to a ' tonally neutral’ category. … Tone 1.— … Features of the utterance: ‘clear’ voice-quality ; simple fall in pitch from high to low. … Tone 2.— … Features of the utterance: breathy, ‘chesty’, ‘hollow’ voice-quality ; … pitch falls to low after a short rise.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 111-113, Study I 'Tone'; list-intonation forms p. 113; word-domain statement p. 116
tone_statements.summary: Two word tones: tone 1 (clear voice; pitch falls from high, high level in lists) vs tone 2 (breathy voice; short rise then fall to low, low rising in lists), Nepali loans toneless.

tone_statements.quote: In their analysis of Gurung, Glover (1970) and Glover and Glover (1977) have stated only one tone system, 'accent' ('high pitch' v. 'low pitch'), supplemented by a category of 'breathiness' ('breathy' v. 'clear'). (p. 53)

tone_statements.summary: Second-hand only (Mazaudon 1978; Glover 1970; Glover and Glover 1977). Sprigg treats Gurung as sharing the TGTM four-term system (register x contour) and equates Glover's clear/breathy with his register tones 1/2. Catalog codes Gurung fixed / pitch accent; this work gives no stress placement, so the stress rule is untouched; its four-tone (Mazaudon) vs accent+breathiness (Glover) framing is report

sources.quote: In Gurung the first syllable of a phonological word seems to be marked by an initial stress (in addition to the contrastive potentials for pitch and breathiness). This stress serves to help divide a phonological phrase into phonological words (or 'feet'). (Glover has tested our early hypothesis that stress may be contrastive throughout the word, but has now rejected this hypothesis.)

sources.quote: This summary of Kaski Gurung (Ghachok, Nepal) is synthesized from several accounts: Glover (1970), Glover et al. (1977), Glover and Landon (1980), Hale (1973), Mazaudon (1978), Sprigg (1997). The system is essentially the same as with Tamang, where tone is based on vowel phonation type (i.e. “register” in accounts of Gurung), and vowel F0 (i.e. “accent”). The correlates are linked; breathy vowels associate with low F0, and modal vowels associate with high F0. In addition, there is a similar consonant onset correspondence seen with Tamang. Voiced onset are found only with breathy vowels, while voiceless aspirated onsets are found only with modal vowels, giving rise to a four-way system, illustrated in Table 3. || Table 3. Gurung tones on monosyllabic roots (Mazaudon 1978: 175–178): /1/ Modal, High and level; /2/ Breathy, High Falling; /3/ Modal Low level/falling; /4/ Breathy Low level/falling (or rise-fall). || An initial analysis by Glover (1970) was that the domain for contrastive tone is the morpheme. However, Hale (1973) noted that a word will have maximally one accent, and vowel phonation is realized only on the initial syllable of a word, no matter the morphological complexity
sources.locator: sec. 2.2.2 Gurung, printed pp. 71-72; Tables 3 and 4 on printed p. 72

sources.quote: There seem to be three identifiable tones: a very low tone that occurs with breathy vowels, a mid-tone with optionally slightly-breathy vowels, and a high tone with clear vowels. sources.quote: In TGTM languages the tone bearing unit in the lexicon is the morpheme; in the sentence, it is the word, formed of a tonal lexical item plus its atonal grammatical affixes. … All languages of the Tamang branch described until now2 exhibit a four-tone system (Mazaudon M., 1978). … Five of the eight dialects listed have a main split in their system between two high tones and two low tones. These are Risiangku and Sahugaon Tamang, Tukche and Syang Thakali, and Ghachok Gurung. Correlatively, the low tones are accompanied by a particular phonation type, which has been described as breathiness

sources.quote: Each monosyllabic word, in languages of the TGTM group, can carry one of four tones. … the languages of the TGTM group do not distinguish four tones on each syllable of a word … but only four tones per word. … In five dialects out of eight, Risiangku and Sahu Tamang, Tukche and Syang Thakali, and Ghachok Gurung, tone-1 and tone-2 words ‘are high with a clear voice quality; tone-3 and tone-4 are low with a breathy voice quality. sources.quote: TT was a "four-box" register language, which means that each word-base (WB) is interpreted as having had two syllables, each of which had back (tense) or front (lax) tongue-root articulation. … Stress, relative pitch, pitch contour, intensity and breathiness carry a high proportion of the functional load of the register system in T, Gu, and Th. the prosodic features of the three languages are realized as follows; … Gu word-bases may be om clear intense, (b) clear relaxed, (3) breathy rising, or (da) breathy low pitch.
